When AI does several steps of a job in a row, where should a person check the work? The question came out of a brief on the paper [*Chaining Tasks, Redefining Work*](/ai-briefs/research-briefs/ai-and-work/chaining-tasks.md). In that paper's model, a person checks only the final output of a run of AI steps. Checking then costs the same however long the run is ([Demirer et al., 2026](#ev-demirer-2026-chain-verification-fixed-cost)). As I read it, that arrangement pays off only if the final check catches mistakes made earlier.

This site already covers two neighboring questions. [When to Let AI Do It](/decision-guides/when-to-let-ai-do-it.md) sets how much of a single task to hand to AI. [The Four Levels of Workflow AI Integration](/enterprise-ai-transformation/tracks/05-workflow-optimization-and-automation/03-the-four-levels-of-workflow-ai-integration.md) explains why errors compound across steps. Neither says where in a sequence of steps the check belongs.

In brief, the evidence says more about where to put a check than about whether one check is enough. Established fields put the check just before the step that commits, where an error becomes costly or permanent. Studies of people reviewing AI output show they often accept its mistakes. That gives reason to doubt that one check at that point catches earlier errors. No study I found tests whether it does.

## Errors build on each other

The simple picture treats each step as an independent chance of failure. Recent measurements suggest errors are not independent. Once a model's record of its own earlier steps contains mistakes, its later steps get less accurate ([Sinha et al., 2026](#ev-sinha-2026-long-horizon-self-conditioning)). In that study, recent models with built-in reasoning did not show this decline. Prompting other models to reason step by step did not stop it.

When a request arrives piece by piece over a conversation, models average 39% worse than when given it at once ([Laban et al., 2025](#ev-laban-2025-multi-turn-lost-no-recovery)). After a wrong turn, they tend not to recover. Reliability also falls quickly as tasks get longer. On software tasks, agents reach 80% success only on tasks a quarter to a sixth as long as those they manage at 50% ([METR, 2025](#ev-metr-2025-time-horizon-80-percent)).

Mistakes inherited from earlier steps often go unnoticed. One test gave agents that operate software screens a task that already contained a mistake. Across four proprietary AI agents, success fell by 39% to 52% the more steps had run since the mistake ([Bu et al., 2026](#ev-bu-2026-gui-agents-inherited-error-depth)). The agents noticed the mistake 34% to 65% of the time ([Bu et al., 2026](#ev-bu-2026-gui-agents-inherited-error-depth)). The authors work at Alibaba, which makes some of the models tested.

AI checkers can often tell that a run went wrong, but rarely find where. Reviewing finished runs with no special instructions, GPT-5.4 found the first error in 14.9% of runs and 5% of hard ones ([Wang et al., 2026](#ev-telbench-2026-first-error-localization)). One company tested an automated checkpoint inside its own agent on a public benchmark. It caught 8 of 40 wrong outputs, one in five, with no false alarms ([Leni, 2026](#ev-leni-2026-verification-checkpoint-catch-rate)). The authors evaluated their own company's system. As I read them, neither result shows an AI checker reliably tracing where a run went wrong.

Checking every step can stop errors from building. One system completed over a million steps with zero errors ([Meyerson et al., 2025](#ev-meyerson-2025-maker-million-steps)). It split the work into single steps, had the AI answer each several times, and took a vote. Its task was a puzzle in which every step has one known right answer. Most business steps do not.

In practice, many deployed agents hand back to a person quickly. In a survey of 86 practitioners, 68% of deployed agents took fewer than 10 steps before a person stepped in ([Pan et al., 2026](#ev-pan-2026-agents-in-production-steps)).

## Reasons to doubt a single final review

One check at the end assumes the reviewer catches what went wrong upstream. Studies of how people review and rely on AI output give reasons for doubt. None of them tests a review at the end of a chain of AI steps; they test review of single outputs.

- **Reviewers absorb the AI's errors.** In a randomized trial, physicians trained in using AI could consult an AI chatbot on six diagnostic cases. Those whose advice had errors planted in three of the six scored 73.3% on diagnostic reasoning, against 84.9% with error-free advice ([Qazi et al., 2025](#ev-qazi-2026-llm-automation-bias-physicians)). Their top-choice diagnoses were right 76.1% of the time, against 90.5% ([Qazi et al., 2025](#ev-qazi-2026-llm-automation-bias-physicians)). The trial has since appeared in the peer-reviewed journal NEJM AI.
- **Their edits drift toward the AI's draft.** Oncologists' GPT-4-assisted replies to patients ended up closer in content to the AI drafts than to replies they wrote alone ([Chen et al., 2024](#ev-chen-2024-llm-patient-messages-adopted)). The authors suggest the doctors may have taken on the model's assessment.
- **Reviewers can feel sure and be wrong.** People using an AI coding assistant wrote less secure code and believed it was more secure ([Perry et al., 2023](#ev-perry-2023-ai-assistant-insecure-code)).
- **Longer explanations persuade.** Longer AI explanations raised people's confidence without raising accuracy ([Steyvers et al., 2025](#ev-steyvers-2025-explanation-length-confidence)).
- **Review often goes unrecorded.** On GitHub, a site where programmers share code, 61.4% of 33,596 code changes submitted by AI agents had no recorded review ([Duma et al., 2026](#ev-duma-2026-ai-pull-requests-unreviewed)).
- **Skill can fade.** Doctors used to an AI aid detected precancerous growths less often in colonoscopies done without it. Their detection rate fell from 28.4% to 22.4% ([Budzyń et al., 2025](#ev-budzyn-2025-colonoscopy-deskilling)).

How the work is shown and overseen matters. People checked step-by-step AI solutions to simple math problems, some right and some with planted errors ([Zhou, Nguyen et al., 2026](#ev-zhou-2026-interactive-reasoning-verification)). They judged them correctly, including finding any faulty step, 73.5% of the time as plain text and 85.6% with the best interactive display. For AI agents working in a web browser, plan-based oversight cut the odds that a planted problem happened by 76% ([Chen et al., 2026](#ev-chen-2026-computer-use-oversight-strategies)). Once a problem reached execution, people blocked only 29 of 138, about 21%, with no clear difference between setups ([Chen et al., 2026](#ev-chen-2026-computer-use-oversight-strategies)).

Only one study I found compared checking along the way with checking at the end. Of 48 participants, 81% preferred checking along the way ([Zhou, Roy et al., 2026](#ev-zhou-2026-when-should-users-check)). It did not measure errors caught.

## Where established fields and AI guidance put the check

Fields that have run high-consequence processes for decades agree on a few principles, and recent AI guidance follows them. None of the sources below tests whether its placement of checks improves results.

- **By consequence, not at every step.** Human factors is the study of how people work with machines. A founding framework in the field limits high automation of decisions and actions to low-risk situations ([Parasuraman et al., 2000](#ev-parasuraman-sheridan-wickens-2000-last-chance)). Singapore's regulator, in non-binding guidance, asks for human approval before high-stakes or irreversible actions, and when an agent behaves unusually ([IMDA, 2026](#ev-imda-2026-agentic-approval-checkpoints)). OpenAI's agent guide calls in a person for high-risk actions and when an agent exceeds its failure limits ([OpenAI, 2025](#ev-openai-2025-agent-human-intervention-triggers)).
- **Just before the action that commits.** The same framework adds a condition. Where the decision itself is highly automated, a person at the action stage is a "last chance opportunity" to trap errors ([Parasuraman et al., 2000](#ev-parasuraman-sheridan-wickens-2000-last-chance)). Surgical teams pause before the first incision ([WHO, 2009](#ev-who-2009-surgical-checklist-pause)). In nuclear plant quality rules, "hold points" stop work until an inspector signs off ([US NRC](#ev-nrc-10cfr50-appb-hold-points)). In Anthropic's framework, its coding agent can read by default but must ask before changing code or systems ([Anthropic, 2025](#ev-anthropic-2025-agents-approval-before-modify)).
- **A separate checker, and limits by amount.** Banking controls require approval above set limits and keep approving a payment apart from making it. They also warn that controls treated as an add-on may be skipped under time pressure ([Basel Committee, 1998](#ev-basel-1998-internal-control-limits)).
- **Checks that fire on triggers.** A UC Berkeley risk guide for AI agents suggests checks can fire after a set amount of activity, such as calls to other software. They can also fire when an agent is asked to act outside its remit ([UC Berkeley CLTC, 2026](#ev-cltc-2026-agentic-checkpoint-triggers)).

Regulations leave placement open. For high-risk systems, the EU AI Act requires oversight in proportion to risk and autonomy, and a way to override or stop the system. It requires confirmation by two people only for systems that identify people remotely by their physical features ([EU AI Act, 2024](#ev-eu-ai-act-2024-article-14-oversight)). The US standards body NIST asks organizations to define their oversight processes and says some systems may not need it ([NIST, 2023](#ev-nist-2023-ai-rmf-human-oversight)).

Two cautions apply. Deciding in advance which actions are consequential may itself be hard ([Feng et al., 2025](#ev-feng-2025-levels-of-autonomy-consequential)). Adding a checkpoint also adds engineering work ([Google Cloud, 2026](#ev-google-cloud-2026-human-in-the-loop-pattern)).

A note on sources: Anthropic, OpenAI and Google all sell agents. I drafted this note with Claude, which Anthropic makes.

## What checking costs

Every check takes time, and the evidence on how much is thin. One economic study argues that near-perfect AI accuracy costs disproportionately more, so keeping people on the remaining work is often cheaper ([Li et al., 2026](#ev-li-thompson-2026-partial-automation)). It was calibrated on computer vision tasks. Another treats people's capacity to check AI work as the binding limit on growth ([Catalini et al., 2026](#ev-catalini-2026-verification-bandwidth)). In that model, deploying unchecked systems can pay for a single firm while hidden risk builds up. A third predicts that workers who are weaker at checking hand too much to AI and check less ([Huang et al., 2026](#ev-huang-2026-delegation-and-verification)).

Measured costs are few. In a randomized trial, experienced developers took 19% longer with AI and spent about 9% of their time reviewing and cleaning its output ([METR, 2025](#ev-metr-2025-review-and-cleaning-time)). In Denmark, chatbot users reported saving 2.8% of work hours on average ([Humlum & Vestergaard, 2025](#ev-humlum-vestergaard-2025-new-review-tasks)). The same study found that chatbots created new tasks for 8.4% of workers, including reviewing AI output. Two vendor surveys of workers' estimates report that checking and fixing AI output uses up much of the time AI saves ([Workday, 2026](#ev-workday-2026-ai-rework); [Foxit, 2026](#ev-foxit-2026-validation-time)).

Getting it wrong has a price too. A British Columbia tribunal held Air Canada liable for wrong information from its customer-facing chatbot ([BC Civil Resolution Tribunal, 2024](#ev-bccrt-2024-moffatt-chatbot-reasonable-care)). The tribunal found the airline had not taken reasonable care to make sure the chatbot was accurate.

## Where the evidence leaves the question

My reading, which the evidence does not settle:

1. **Check before any step that is costly or hard to undo.** That means sending, paying, deleting, publishing or changing an important record. The established fields agree on this, and the AI guidance points the same way.
2. **Do not count on that check to catch a mistake made earlier.** In the physician trial, errors planted in the AI's advice lowered doctors' diagnostic scores ([Qazi et al., 2025](#ev-qazi-2026-llm-automation-bias-physicians)). I expect the same at the end of a chain, though no study tests it. Where an early step feeds everything after it, check that step's output too.
3. **Make the check a required step the work cannot skip.** Checks treated as extras can be skipped under time pressure. Where the stakes justify it, give the check to someone other than the person who ran the work.
4. **Check selectively, guided by consequence.** Every check costs time, and the Workday and Foxit surveys report that checking uses up much of what AI saves ([Workday, 2026](#ev-workday-2026-ai-rework); [Foxit, 2026](#ev-foxit-2026-validation-time)).

This is more cautious than the model behind *Chaining Tasks*, which assumes the final check works. Where checks go is one part of the wider question in [Rethink the Process, or Just Add AI?](/research-notes/rethink-the-process-or-just-add-ai.md).

### Still open

- Does an end-of-job review catch an early error hidden in a polished result? I found no study that tests it.
- Does checking step by step catch more errors than checking at the end? The one comparison I found measured preference, not errors caught.
- Where do organizations actually put their checks, and what happens? I found no firm-level evidence.
- What does a check cost against the errors it prevents? No study I found measures both.
- Does checking every step, as in the million-step puzzle study, work when a step has no single right answer?
